1079.title: The chained woman
1079.hook: a woman whose husband won't grant a divorce; every stream seeks solutions
1079.howItsDone: Orthodox couples may sign a halachic prenuptial agreement and rabbinical courts may press a husband to give a get; Conservative ketubot may include an added clause; Reform Judaism generally accepts civil divorce; and Jewish groups across the streams campaign for women who are refused a get.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the get, the written document of divorce, and your line: even the altar weeps. Today, a new week, and the other side of that document.

Rabbi Akiva is far from home, in Nehardea in Babylonia. A man there pulls him aside with a teaching he's been carrying. In the land of Israel, he's heard, only one sage lets a woman remarry on the word of a single witness that her husband has died. Go back, the man says, and tell them in my name. Akiva carries it home and repeats it before Rabban Gamaliel, and Gamaliel is glad. The Mishnah says the rule was then set: one witness is enough. Why would a court bend its own rules of evidence? Because of the woman waiting.
screen: `AKIVA IN NEHARDEA.` → `TELL THEM IN MY NAME.` → `ONE WITNESS IS ENOUGH.`

segments.voice: Agunah. The word is usually translated the chained woman. In Jewish law a marriage ends with a get, a document the husband gives. The shadow side: without a get, she can't remarry under Jewish law. First, the old case: the husband who vanished. A man goes to sea, or to war, and never comes back. No body, no document. Is she a widow or a wife? Normally a court wants two witnesses. For her, the rabbis accepted one, and the Talmud gives the reason in a phrase: they were lenient because of the agunah. The law bent to free her. Second, the modern case: the husband who refuses. He's alive, the marriage is over, and he won't give the get, sometimes to punish her, sometimes to bargain. She's chained by his choice. Third, the answers, and each stream works in its own way. In Orthodox communities, rabbinical courts can pressure a refusing husband, and some couples now sign a prenuptial agreement that makes refusal costly. Conservative rabbis added a clause to the ketubah, and their courts have other tools. Reform Judaism generally accepts a civil divorce, so this bind doesn't arise there in the same way. And across the streams, women and rabbis have gone public, standing outside the homes and workplaces of men who refuse, asking them to give the get. Different paths, the same direction. Akiva's single witness shows how the tradition's own rules can bend toward a woman who's waiting.

If anyone is in danger, call or text 988 in the US, or local emergency help, any hour.

1080.title: Damages
1080.hook: the fourth order: civil law, courts, and Pirkei Avot
1080.howItsDone: The tractates of Nezikin are studied in yeshivas and daf yomi classes, and rabbinical courts draw on them in civil disputes; Pirkei Avot is studied in some communities on Shabbat afternoons, often in the weeks between Passover and Shavuot.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the agunah, and a court that bent its own rules to free her. Your line: unchain her. Today, the fourth order of the Mishnah.

A neighbor's tree drops its branches over your wall. A borrowed cow dies in the borrower's barn. Two people walk into court holding the same cloak, each saying, it's mine, I found it. A worker wants his wages before sundown. These are the cases waiting in the fourth order of the Mishnah, and it reads like small claims court. Then, among the tractates on courts and oaths, there's one with no lawsuits at all: just sayings of the sages about how to live.
screen: `A TREE OVER THE WALL.` → `TWO PEOPLE, ONE CLOAK.` → `SAYINGS AMONG THE LAWSUITS.`

segments.voice: Nezikin. Damages. Here's the order, room by room. First, the gates. It opens with three tractates called Bava Kamma, Bava Metzia and Bava Batra: the first gate, the middle gate and the last gate. Between them they cover harm done, things lost and found, loans and wages, buying and selling, neighbors and property lines. Ordinary life, where people bump into each other and someone gets hurt. Second, the courts. Tractate Sanhedrin sets out who judges, how witnesses are questioned, and how carefully a court must move when a life is at stake. The Torah's line stands behind it all, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "Justice, justice shalt thou follow." Third, the sayings. Tractate Avot, also called Pirkei Avot, opens with a chain of teachers handing down the Torah, and the first advice it records is be deliberate in judgment. Its first chapter ends with a teaching that the world stands on three things: justice, truth and peace. Some readers say Avot sits here because judges need character, not only rules. A court is only as fair as the people in it. Fourth, the mistake. The order also holds Horayot, a tractate on what happens when the court itself rules wrongly and people follow it. The law plans for its own judges getting it wrong. So Nezikin says something plain. Justice isn't a slogan. It's a tree branch, a dead cow, a cloak, a wage, handled carefully, by people trying to be good, who know they can be wrong.

1081.title: Ox, pit, fire (Bava Kamma 2a)
1081.hook: the Mishnah opens with four main causes of damage
1081.howItsDone: Bava Kamma is often among the first tractates studied in yeshivas, and its categories of damage are still applied by rabbinical courts in civil disputes between Jews who bring their cases there.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nezikin, the order of damages: three gates, the courts, and Avot beside them. Your line: damages and justice. Today, through the first gate.

An ox wanders out of its yard and tramples a neighbor's garden. A man digs a pit in a public path, leaves it open, and someone's donkey falls in. A farmer lights a fire to burn off his stubble, the wind shifts, and the flames jump into the next field. Three scenes from a farming village, ordinary and a little awful. They're also the opening of the first gate, tractate Bava Kamma. Before it says anything about money, the Mishnah names the culprits.
screen: `AN OX IN THE GARDEN.` → `A PIT LEFT OPEN.` → `FIRE ON THE WIND.`

segments.voice: Ox. Bava Kamma opens: there are four fathers of damage, the ox, the pit, a third that the Talmud argues over, and the fire. You've heard fathers before: last week, the fathers of work on Shabbat. Same idea here: main categories, with offspring that grow from them. First, each one comes from the Torah. The goring ox, and the animal let loose to graze in someone else's field. The pit, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "if a man shall dig a pit and not cover it." The fire: "he that kindled the fire shall surely make restitution." Second, the third father is a puzzle. The Mishnah gives it a short, hard word, and in the Talmud one sage says it means a person, another says the tooth, an animal eating what isn't its owner's. Third, what makes them different? An ox moves on its own. A pit just sits there. Fire has no life at all, yet it travels. Each causes harm in its own way, so you can't learn one from another. Fourth, what they share, and that's the heart of it. It's their way to do damage, and guarding them is on you. You didn't trample the garden; your ox did. You didn't push the donkey; your pit was open. You didn't burn the field; your fire went where fires go. What you set loose in the world, you answer for. And an ox with a history of goring, the Torah adds, puts even more on its owner, who was warned.

1082.title: Lost and found
1082.hook: finders must announce and return what they find
1082.howItsDone: Jews who keep halacha treat returning lost property as a commandment, announcing finds that carry identifying signs and returning them when an owner describes them; some synagogues and communities keep lost-and-found notices for this reason.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ox, the pit and the fire: what you set loose in the world, you answer for. Your line: four causes of damage. Today, a glove on a fence post.

A single glove, hung on a fence post at eye level. Someone found it on the sidewalk and put it where its owner might walk back past. A small, wordless kindness, and the Torah has words for it. Deuteronomy says that if you see your neighbor's ox or sheep wandering off, you bring it back. Then the circle widens: a donkey, a garment, anything your neighbor lost and you found. And the passage ends with a short line, in the old JPS translation: "thou mayest not hide thyself."
screen: `A GLOVE ON A FENCE POST.` → `THE OX, THE GARMENT, ANY LOST THING.` → `THOU MAYEST NOT HIDE THYSELF.`

segments.voice: Hashavat aveidah. Returning a lost thing. Start with what the verse forbids. Not stealing; that's covered elsewhere. It forbids hiding yourself: looking away, walking past as if you hadn't seen. This commandment begins in the eyes. The Mishnah, in the tractate Bava Metzia, builds that line into a working system. First: which finds do you have to announce? The answer turns on signs, simanim in Hebrew. Coins scattered loose on a road carry nothing to tell them apart, so the finder may keep them. But money in a purse, fruit in a basket, a thing with a mark on it: those must be announced, because someone can say, that's mine, and here's how I know. Second, the announcing. The Mishnah records a debate between rabbis over how long to keep announcing, and the Talmud remembers a stone in Jerusalem where finds were proclaimed and owners came to claim them. Third, who gets it back? Not whoever shouts loudest. The claimant describes the signs, and if they match, it goes home. Behind it all sits a question the Talmud turns over at length: when has an owner given up? The rabbis call it yeush, despair. So the system holds two people in view: the owner's hope and the finder's honesty. A law about gloves and purses is also a law about attention. For a little while, your neighbor's loss is your job.

1083.title: Two hold a cloak (Bava Metzia 2a)
1083.hook: two people claim one garment; each swears, and they divide it
1083.tomorrow: A court that almost never executed
1083.howItsDone: Some students of the Talmud begin with Bava Metzia, whose opening case of two people holding one garment is studied line by line in yeshivas and study partnerships.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hashavat aveidah: don't look away from what your neighbor lost. Your line: return it. Today, two people holding one cloak.

One cloak, and two fists closed on it. Not tugging. Just holding. One says: I found it, it's all mine. The other says: I found it, it's all mine. There are no witnesses, no receipt, and no window into either heart. This is the case that opens the tractate Bava Metzia, the middle gate of the laws of damages and dealings. So what does a court do when both stories sound exactly the same?
screen: `ONE CLOAK, TWO FISTS.` → `I FOUND IT. I FOUND IT.` → `NO WITNESSES.`

segments.voice: Two hold a cloak. The Mishnah's ruling is short. Each one swears that they own no less than half of it, and they divide. Look at what that oath does. Neither swears it's all theirs. Each swears only to the part that could be true for both at once. The court doesn't pretend to know what it can't know. Then the Mishnah changes the case. One says, it's all mine. The other says, half of it is mine. Now the first swears to no less than three quarters, the second to no less than a quarter. The one claiming half has already granted the other half, so only one half is really in dispute, and only that half gets split. The rule isn't split everything down the middle. It's split what's actually contested. The Talmud lingers over these few lines. One question it asks: if they're dividing anyway, why make anyone swear? One answer: so that nobody grabs a stranger's cloak in the street, says it's mine, and hopes to walk off with half. The oath makes a grab cost something. Read it once more and three pieces of a fair process show through. Hear both sides as equals. Divide only what's truly in dispute. Make lying expensive. And none of it depends on knowing who's right. A court that admits what it can't see.

1084.title: A court that almost never executed (Mishnah Makkot 1:10)
1084.hook: a court that executed once in seven years was called destructive; some said once in seventy
1084.howItsDone: Jews study the tractates Sanhedrin and Makkot as part of the Talmud's order of damages, and the debate in Makkot 1:10 is often cited in Jewish discussions of justice and the death penalty.

segments.voice: Yesterday, two hold a cloak: no witnesses, so each swears to half and they divide. Your line: each takes half. Today, a court that leans toward life.

A court that puts someone to death once in seven years is called destructive. That's a sentence from the Mishnah, in the tractate Makkot, and it comes from inside the system, from the rabbis who taught the laws of the court. Then another voice: Rabbi Eleazar ben Azariah says, once in seventy years. Then Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva say: if we had sat on the court, no one would ever have been put to death.
screen: `ONCE IN SEVEN YEARS: DESTRUCTIVE.` → `SOME SAY SEVENTY.` → `WE WOULD NEVER HAVE EXECUTED.`

segments.voice: Sanhedrin. The Mishnah's name for the great court, and the name of the tractate that lays out how it works. The Torah does name crimes that carry death. The Mishnah keeps those laws, then builds a court that leans hard the other way. Three of its rules. First, the order of speaking. Capital cases open with reasons to acquit, not to convict, and anyone may argue for the accused. Second, the clock. Acquittal may be given the same day. A verdict of guilt waits until the next day, so the judges sleep on it. Third, the road. The Mishnah describes someone at the door of the court with a cloth in hand, and a rider posted at a distance. If anyone comes forward with something in the accused's favor, the cloth waves, the rider gallops off, and the procession stops. Even on the way out, the case can reopen. Then the argument in Makkot: seven years, seventy, never. And the Mishnah doesn't let that last word stand alone. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel answers Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva: then you would multiply murderers in Israel. A court that never acts doesn't protect anyone either. Both voices stay on the page. Some readers take all this as a memory of how courts once ran; others, as a picture of what a court ought to be. Either way, when a life hangs in the balance, the system tilts toward keeping it.

Your line: lean toward life. In the Mishnah's court, mercy gets the first word. Until tomorrow.

1085.title: Warning the witnesses (Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5)
1085.hook: witnesses in capital cases were told that one life is a whole world
1085.howItsDone: Jews study Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5 as part of the Talmud's order of damages, and its line about saving one life as saving a whole world is quoted in Jewish teaching, memorials and ethics.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sanhedrin: acquittal argued first, and a cloth that can stop the procession. Your line: lean toward life. Today, what the court says before a witness speaks.

The witnesses are brought into the room. A life may depend on what they're about to say. So the court doesn't start with questions. It starts with a speech. The Mishnah, in the tractate Sanhedrin, gives it almost line by line, and it's surprising. It doesn't quote a penalty for lying. It tells a story about the first human being, and about coins.
screen: `BEFORE A WORD IS SAID.` → `NOT A THREAT: A SPEECH.` → `THE FIRST HUMAN, AND COINS.`

segments.voice: Warning the witnesses. You met part of this speech back in year one; today, see the court put it to work. It moves in four steps. First, the court names the easy mistakes. Perhaps you're speaking from guesswork. Perhaps from hearsay, one witness repeating another, or from someone you trust. None of that is testimony. Second, the weight. A money case can be repaired with money. A life case can't. The court points to Cain, and to God's words to him, in the old JPS translation: "the voice of thy brother's blood crieth unto Me from the ground." In Hebrew, the Mishnah notes, the word is plural: bloods. His blood, and the blood of every child he would have had. Third, the line people still repeat. Only a single human being was created at the start, to teach that whoever destroys one life is counted as if they destroyed a whole world, and whoever sustains one life, as if they sustained a whole world. Fourth, the coins. A person stamps many coins from one seal, and they all come out alike. But every human being is stamped from the seal of the first human, and not one is like another. So each person must be able to say: the world was created for my sake. A witness is about to describe one person. The court wants them to see, first, that they're describing a world.
screen: `NOT GUESSWORK, NOT HEARSAY.` · `BLOODS: THE CHILDREN WHO WOULD HAVE BEEN.` · `ONE LIFE, A WHOLE WORLD.` · `ONE SEAL, AND NO TWO ALIKE.` · then, large: `A WHOLE WORLD.`
